    #101448. Latest Update: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2218 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio.
    • In a recent development, the station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    In a recent development, the station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he mentioned was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    It has been revealed that the previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Recent findings suggest that two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    Industry observers note that at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Sources indicate that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Recent findings suggest that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    Brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and stated he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    It has been revealed that brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    It has been revealed that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    Sources indicate that brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    It has been revealed that in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    At the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    According to recent reports, in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    It has been revealed that the case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws highlights the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    #101446. 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1090 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.
    • Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences.
    • Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an important glitch: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.

    Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences. At nearly the same time, a lawsuit challenging admissions to the county’s middle school magnet programs reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

    Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an important glitch: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?

    Sources indicate that the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice recognized Minorities in Magnets, directed by Toftaa Fedhaa, as the first place winner of the section’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition. Her film explores the experiences of students of color in the Montgomery County Public Schools’ high school magnet programs and the effects of their underrepresentation.

    Separately, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case concerns admissions to four selective middle school magnet programs, not the high school programs discussed in the film.

    While the court did not rule on whether the district’s admissions policy is discriminatory, it agreed to consider a narrower legal question about the evidence plaintiffs must present when challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory.

    Recent findings suggest that the Association for Education Fairness alleges that Montgomery County’s admissions policies intentionally disadvantaged Asian American students. The school district maintains that its admissions system is designed to provide equitable access to rigorous educational opportunities.

    After initially challenging a “field test,” the plaintiffs challenged a revised lottery-based system introduced for the 2021-2022 school year. That system screened students for their potential to benefit from enriched instruction and then used a lottery to assign students to magnet programs or enriched instruction at their neighborhood schools.

    The federal district court dismissed the challenge to the revised initiative, finding that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged discriminatory effect or intent. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, affirmed, applying circuit precedent on disparate impact allegations.

    The Supreme Court will now consider whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy must demonstrate that the affected group experienced an aggregate “disparate impact” compared with its share of the applicant pool.

    Industry observers note that put simply, “disparate impact” refers to a policy that produces unequal outcomes for a particular group, even when the policy does not expressly classify individuals by race. An equal protection challenge also raises the question of discriminatory purpose.

    The court’s decision will address the legal standards governing these types of claims and whether a particular showing of aggregate impact is required before such a claim may proceed, not whether Montgomery County’s policy ultimately violates the Constitution. The court has not yet decided the merits of the case.

    The film underscores why the conversation should not only focus exclusively on admissions policies, statistics and legal standards but should also consider the voices and experiences of students.

    The file and the lawsuit should not be confused or treated as evidence of one another. They involve different grade levels, programs and legal questions. The experiences described in the film do not establish what happened in the middle school admissions process, just as the allegations in the lawsuit do not resolve the concerns raised by high school students.

    Although selective educational programs can open doors to advanced coursework, specialized instruction and opportunities that shape a student’s academic future, simply making a program available to everyone does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to participate.

    We must also consider who knows these programs exist, how students are identified and encouraged to apply, what barriers may discourage participation, and whether students feel represented and welcome once they are admitted.

    In a recent development, these are notable questions for educators, families, policymakers and communities to consider. They may also inform legal analysis, although the applicable legal standards determine what evidence is relevant to a particular claim.

    For lawyers, the Supreme Court case highlights the importance of understanding how statistical evidence, applicant pools and allegations of discriminatory intent intersect when challenging facially neutral policies. It also reinforces the need to examine the specific admissions process and how that process may have changed over time. The court’s decision may affect how courts evaluate statistical evidence in challenges to facially neutral admissions policies.

    For school officials, families and advocates, the broader questions are equally vital:.

    • How are students identified and informed about selective educational opportunities?

    • What criteria determine eligibility and admission?

    • Are admissions outcomes regularly examined across schools and student populations?

    • Are the policies and measures used to assess access transparent and understandable?

    These questions deserve attention regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately resolves the legal problem before it.

    The case is also a reminder that we must distinguish between allegations in a lawsuit, a school district’s stated reasons for its policies, procedural court decisions, and a final ruling on the merits. Understanding those distinctions is essential to an informed discussion.

    In a recent development, the winning film, Minorities in Magnets, brings student perspectives into a debate that is often reduced to admissions criteria and demographic statistics. The Supreme Court will address a specific legal question about the evidence required in an equal protection challenge.

    Recent findings suggest that neither alone answers the broader question of what meaningful educational opportunity should look like. But they invite a broader conversation about how communities define opportunity, how they measure access, and how they respond when students say the system is not working for them.

    As lawyers and members of our communities, we have an obligation to listen, ask difficult questions, and examine whether the systems we create are providing genuine opportunities for all students.

    In a recent development, ultimately, educational access is about more than who gets admitted. It is also about who gets the opportunity to succeed, who feels that they belong, and whether every student has a fair chance to reach their full potential.

    Recent findings suggest that mario A. Sulllivan is the immediate past chair of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice and a name partner at Johnson & Sullivan in Chicago.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    #101443. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (266 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (266 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    âI understand why the conversation went the way it did at the initial hearings, the government has had weeks and weeks to scour all his accounts, all his devices, and they don’t have anything to prove his serious risk of flight,â he noted.

However, the district decided to not bury the new power lines underground or otherwise protect them. As a result, the plaintiffs say, the lines melted during the 2025 blaze, rendering the recent improvements all but worthless.

    “They elected to choose a system that was not resistant to fire occurring,” plaintiffs’ attorney Peter McNulty told the judge at a hearing Tuesday. “If you get money and design a system, you canât cheap out and not protect that system.”.

    He later added: “To not do that, that is a failure they caused to occur. Itâs not just that a couple of conduits melted. Itâs that the whole system didnât deliver the protection it was supposed to.”.

    Last week, a federal jury convicted 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht, a former Uber drier, of two counts of arson for setting the Lachman Fire shortly after midnight on New Yearâs Day, 2025. That relatively small brush fire was easily suppressed, but remained smoldering and reignited into the much larger Palisades Fire thanks to especially dry conditions and strong winds.

    In a recent development, much of the plaintiffs’ master complaint focuses on the state of California and the city of Los Angeles and what they claim is their failure to monitor the area of the Lachman Fire, and for not adequately managing the vegetation in the area. They also fault the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power for leaving the 117-million-gallon Santa Ynez Reservoir empty.

    Their claims also include inverse condemnation against the county and the water district, for the unprotected power lines. Mira Hashmall, the attorney representing the county, argued inverse condemnation can only apply to public improvements that damage private property âÂ and not public improvements that don’t do a good enough job of protecting the public.

    It has been revealed that “It’s not intended for loosey-goosey concepts of negligence,” Hasmall mentioned. Should the plaintiffs’ theory become the standard, she said, “public entities would become insurers” and “disincentive creative backup intends that may not work.”.

    Jessner did not say when she would matter a final ruling.

    After the hearing, McNulty said the claim against the county was a small but significant part of the case, “but weâll live to fight another day if the judge sticks with her tentative.”.

    Industry News: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Industry observers note that on November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Industry observers note that on November 10, The Newly introduced York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    The Times story has reverberated promptly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and important source.

    Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “mentioned in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    According to recent reports, rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    So how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam said that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    From there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at problem is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    In a recent development, this test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    In a recent development, this is particularly relevant since the court is currently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    Recommended Citation: Andrew Willinger, The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-second-amendment-and-an-unusually-dangerous-approach-to-dicta/.

    Recent findings suggest that SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â San Francisco’s reparations fund is empty. Still, a taxpayer rights group is urging a Superior Court judge to rule that the city’s reparations plan is unconstitutional.

    In a recent development, an attorney for the nonprofit Californians for Equal Rights Foundation and two of its members argued in front of San Francisco Superior Court Judge A. Marisa Chun Tuesday that racial classifications for funds appropriated with taxpayer money are unlawful.

    Plaintiffsâ attorney Andrew Quinio mentioned even though the reparations fund is presently empty, the threat of unlawfully distributing taxpayer money is still possible, as the San Francisco Board of Supervisors has neither rescinded the initiative nor changed the underlying law that details the racial language that guides the way the money should be used.

    According to recent reports, âThere is no other description other than one that is race-based,â Quinio mentioned about the strategy for the reparations fund. âIt outlines a variety of methods to provide restitution, compensation and rehabilitation to individuals who are Black â¦ and have experienced the proven harm in San Francisco.".

    Quinio noted the city made a deliberate choice about how it defined the reparations initiative.

    âIt chose a specific racial category that canât be ignored; that language isnât inconsequential and under Connerly racial classifications are immediately suspect,â he said, citing a 2001 California Court of Appeal decision in Connerly v. State Personnel Board, ruling race- and gender-based preferences and classifications in state contracting, education and civil service violated equal protection principles.

    San Francisco Deputy City Attorney John George countered Quinioâs arguments, saying the city hasnât allocated funds unlawfully, because it hasnât given any money through the fund at all. To do so, he said, even donations under $10,000 would need approval by the Board of Supervisors as to where the money should go.

    Furthermore, George said, the fund could be used in several ways, with over 150 recommendations for the fundâs administrator, the San Francisco Human Rights Commission, to consider, including race-neutral options such as updating technology at all San Francisco Unified School District schools.

    Sources indicate that in June, Superior Court Judge Joseph Quinn, sustained a demurrer against the plaintiffs’ first complaint, ruling the lawsuit was not ripe. Chun, who is considering the plaintiffs’ amended complaint, asked Quinio Tuesday if the threat of funds going out unlawfully was imminent.

    âAt least, sitting here in San Francisco, I just donât get the sense that the city is going to be cutting $5 million checks to people based upon allegedly their protected status, their race," Chun said.

    In rebuttal, Quinio said that while the threat of large sums going into the fund may not be imminent, the cityâs general fund positioned the Human Rights Commission to administer the reparations fund when it is ready.

    Recent findings suggest that âEven though thereâs no funds in the account, the city doesnât lose responsibility or management of the fund. The same way one doesnât lose power over their bank account because thereâs no money in it.â.

    In a recent development, san Francisco established the African American Reparations Advisory Committee in 2020. In July 2023, the committee published theÂ San Francisco Reparations Blueprint, which comprised recommendations on how to address the historical harms faced by Black San Franciscans due to the legacy of enslavement. Recommendations included issuing a formal apology for past harms, committing to investments in the Black community and creating an independent Office of Reparations to track implementation of the reparations plan.

    The cityâs Board of SupervisorsÂ voted to acceptÂ the plan in October 2023. Two years later, in December 2025, theyÂ unanimously votedÂ to establish the San Francisco Reparations Fund, and San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie signed the ordinance into law on Dec. 23 of that year.

    âThe passage of this ordinance moves San Francisco from apology to action," District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton said in aÂ statementÂ after the ordinance was passed.

    âFor years, Black San Franciscans have been clear that recognition without resources is not enough," he added.

    At the beginning of Tuesdayâs hearing, Chun was prepared to adopt her tentative ruling, sustaining the cityâs demurrer without leave to amend. However, by the end of the hour-long proceeding, she told the attorneys she needed to look further into some of the cases Quinio cited and would write up a fresh tentative ruling.

    âI just need to dig in deeper with these cases,â she stated.

    According to recent reports, A hearing is tentatively scheduled for Jan. 6, 2027.

    Breaking: Firm loses exclusive right to salvage remains of 1875 steamboat disaster

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In four years with exclusive salvage rights, Rockfish has only recovered a firebrick and wood from the wreck site.
    • Industry observers note that SEATTLE (CN) â Loaded with wealthy passengers, opium and gold, the S.S.
    • More than 150 years later, the hunt for treasure is now open game after a companyâs attempt to retain exclusive rights to salvage the wreckage faltered in federal court Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In four years with exclusive salvage rights, Rockfish has only recovered a firebrick and wood from the wreck site.

    Industry observers note that SEATTLE (CN) â Loaded with wealthy passengers, opium and gold, the S.S. Pacific disappeared under the rough waters off the coast of Washington in 1875, never to be found.

    More than 150 years later, the hunt for treasure is now open game after a companyâs attempt to retain exclusive rights to salvage the wreckage faltered in federal court Tuesday.

    Industry observers note that in 2022, the exploration company Rockfish claimed it had located the remains of a vessel believed to be the S.S. Pacific: a 223-foot sidewheel steamer that sank on Nov. 4, 1875, after colliding with another vessel 80 miles south of Cape Flattery, Washington.

    Industry observers note that it took less than an hour for the Pacific to sink, killing more than 300 people believed to be on board. Just before sinking, the Pacific picked up prominent and wealthy passengers in Victoria, Canada, along with a crowd of gold miners from British Columbia. The maritime disaster remains one of the deadliest in U.S. Pacific coast history.

    Rockfish filed an action in federal court that year to secure exclusive salvage rights to the site. U.S. District Judge James Robart granted the request.

    It has been revealed that in late 2023, Robart granted the companyâs motion for an injunction, giving it exclusive right to salvage the shipwreck within a certain boundary through mid-2025. The judge expanded the geographic boundary in 2024 and hesitantly extended the injunction in 2025.

    In that order extending exclusive salvage rights, Robart noted the court was âconcerned with the pace of Rockfishâs salvage efforts,â though he believed the companyâs efforts âremain clothed with some prospect of success.â.

    Industry observers note that but that conclusion changed, with the George W. Bush appointee stripping exclusive rights from the company Tuesday.

    Industry observers note that donald Foster, the great-grandson of one of the Pacificâs passengers, requested the court dissolve the injunction granting Rockfish exclusive salvor rights in October. Foster argued the firm hadnât produced any recovery of identifiable artifacts in the nearly four years it has been running expeditions.

    Industry observers note that prior to gaining salvage rights, Rockfish produced a firebrick and some wood it claimed were recovered from the Pacific. No other artifacts have been reported since.

    Rockfish argued the recoveries constitute âsuccess in part,â an element required to succeed on a maritime salvage claim. But Robart was not convinced.

    According to recent reports, âThe court agrees with Mr. Foster that Rockfish has not demonstrated success in whole or in part and is thus not entitled to a salvage award,â Robart wrote.

    Earlier this month, Rockfish reported to the court that it has completed 20 expeditions to the wreck site and explained several bases for identifying the site as the remains of the Pacific. Robart noted the tech giant admitted it has not recovered any additional artifacts beyond the firebrick and wood that were obtained before filing the lawsuit.

    Foster argued the company neglected to explain why it has failed to recover any of the 450 objects it claims to have mapped on the seafloor, a point with which Robart agreed.

    âUnder settled admiralty law, locating, identifying, and exploring a sunken vessel â however diligently â does not constitute salvage success absent the actual recovery and preservation of imperiled property,â Robart wrote.

    The firm also failed on its law of finds claims for the same reasons its salvage claim failed: âHaving recovered nothing beyond a firebrick and wood over 20 expeditions, Rockfish has failed to present competent evidence that it has reduced the vessel or its cargo to actual or constructive possession â much less to establish that any unrecovered property on the seabed has been abandoned by its owners.â.

    Since the court granted summary judgment against Rockfish on its salvage claim, there was no longer a predicate for keeping the companyâs exclusive salvor status and Robart dissolved the injunction.

    While Foster challenged Rockfishâs salvage claims, he didnât challenge the companyâs claimed title since he has no ownership interest in it, allowing it to proceed as the companyâs sole remaining claim.

    Robart acknowledged that the dismissals of the other claims, however, raise serious questions about whether the court retains subject-matter jurisdiction.

    Neither Rockfish nor Foster responded to a request for comment before press time.

    Supreme Court considers whether bans on semiautomatic rifles violate Second Amendment

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supreme Court declined to take up a case challenging Maryland’s prohibition on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles, with three justices dissenting from the denial of review and a fourth, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, stopping just short of that.
    • “Given that millions of Americans own AR–15s and that a significant majority of the states allow possession of those rifles, [the challengers] have a strong argument that AR–15s are in ‘common use’ by law-abiding citizens and therefore are protected by the Second Amendment under [District of Columbia v.] Heller,” Kavanaugh wrote in a statement respecting the denial.
    • Heller is the court’s landmark 2008 decision that upheld the right of individuals to keep a firearm in the home for self-defense and established that the Second Amendment must be interpreted in light of constitutional text, history and tradition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 24, 2026, 11:12 am CST.

    In June 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up a case challenging Maryland’s prohibition on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles, with three justices dissenting from the denial of review and a fourth, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, stopping just short of that.

    “Given that millions of Americans own AR–15s and that a significant majority of the states allow possession of those rifles, [the challengers] have a strong argument that AR–15s are in ‘common use’ by law-abiding citizens and therefore are protected by the Second Amendment under [District of Columbia v.] Heller,” Kavanaugh wrote in a statement respecting the denial.

    Heller is the court’s landmark 2008 decision that upheld the right of individuals to keep a firearm in the home for self-defense and established that the Second Amendment must be interpreted in light of constitutional text, history and tradition.

    Kavanaugh suggested the court might be assisted in addressing such bans in the future by rulings in pending challenges to similar state laws in several federal appeals courts.

    “Additional petitions for certiorari will likely be before this court shortly, and, in my view, this court should and presumably will address the AR–15 issue soon, in the next term or two,” he wrote.

    According to recent reports, kavanaugh was right on both counts. Next week, the justices will hear arguments in two cases raising the constitutionality of AR-15s “and similar semiautomatic rifles.”.

    “This case has big stakes, symbolically,” says Adam Winkler, a professor at the University of California at Los Angeles School of Law and the author of the 2011 book Gunfight: The Battle Over the Right to Bear Arms in America.

    “The assault weapons bans have been at the very center of the gun debate ever since the Newtown shooting in 2012,” he states, referring to the mass shooting at the Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, in which a perpetrator using an AR-15-style rifle killed 20 first graders and six school staff members.

    “This is the first time the Supreme Court is ruling on the availability of such a high-profile firearm,” Winkler indicates.

    According to recent reports, on Dec. 2, the Supreme Court will take up a challenge to Connecticut’s move, soon after the Sandy Hook mass shooting, to outlaw AR-15 and similar platform semiautomatic rifles. That case, Grant v. Higgins, is consolidated with the lead case, Khaya v. Cook County, in which the justices will consider a 1993 ordinance in prohibiting AR-15-style rifles in Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago.

    In practical terms, the Cook County ordinance has been superseded by an Illinois statute enacted after a mass shooting at the 2022 Fourth of July parade in the Chicago suburb of Highland Park, in which seven people were killed and 50 wounded.

    Besides Connecticut and Illinois, 11 other states prohibit AR-15-style weapons, and the fate of those laws are on the table in the consolidated cases before the justices.

    The Connecticut law was challenged by two gun rights groups and several individuals, who argue that both Heller and the high court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen necessitated a finding that AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are protected arms that cannot be banned consistent with the Second Amendment.

    (Bruen held that the states could not prevent law-abiding citizens with self-defense needs from carrying firearms in public, and it reiterated Heller’s history and tradition test.).

    Industry observers note that the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Latest York upheld Connecticut’s law in 2025, saying governments may restrict weapons that were “unusually dangerous.”.

    Sources indicate that the decades-old Cook County ordinance was challenged in 2021. The 7th Circuit at Chicago in 2025 applied its own 2023 decision that preliminarily upheld the Illinois statute.

    The Trump administration, which is supporting the challenges in the Supreme Court, cites statistics that at least 16 million Americans own AR-15s, and that some 28 million such rifles are in circulation in the country.

    The challengers cite the 16 million figure but also other statistics suggesting that as many as 26 million Americans own AR-15s or similar weapons.

    “If the Second Amendment is to have any teeth at all, at bare minimum, it must include protecting the most common arms in the country,” says Bill Sack, the senior director of legal operations for the Second Amendment Foundation, a Bellevue, Washington-based group that is a plaintiff in and the chief organizer of the Connecticut and Cook County cases.

    The challengers argue that no valid historical principle under the analytical test unveiled in Heller and refined in Bruen justifies the bans on AR-15-style rifles.

    “Our litigation strategy … is making sure that the types of arms that Americans choose to use for all lawful purposes are available to them,” Sack notes. “Long guns … are just as important to the exercise of the Second Amendment as handguns are.”.

    It has been revealed that erin E. Murphy, a partner with Clement & Murphy who helped win the Bruen case, indicates there is another vital way for the court to look at history in the case.

    It has been revealed that “Semiautomatic rifles and semiautomatic handguns have been around for well over a century,” indicates Murphy, who wrote an amicus brief for the National Shooting Sports Foundation in support of the challengers. “I think that history is going to matter to the court.”.

    Connecticut cites the string of deadly mass shootings at schools and other places involving AR-15-style weapons.

    “Tragically, real-world experience confirms the AR-15’s singular dangerousness: From Sandy Hook to Las Vegas to Parkland to Uvalde, shooters have used the AR-15 or similar weapons in the vast majority of mass-casualty shootings this century,” claims the merits brief filed by William Tong, the Connecticut attorney general, and Elizabeth B. Prelogar, a former U.S. solicitor general.

    It has been revealed that while serving under then-President Joe Biden, Prelogar argued United States v. Rahimi, in which the court in 2024 upheld a federal ban on firearm possession by individuals subject to domestic violence restraining orders. Though hired by Connecticut, Prelogar will represent both that state and Cook County in oral arguments before the court.

    Connecticut argues that legislatures going back to medieval England have chosen to ban unusually dangerous weapons, such as English crossbows, colonial trap guns and 19th century Bowie knives.

    “Over the centuries, the march of technological advancement has increased the lethality of weapons, and governments have consistently responded by outlawing weapons with characteristics that make them more lethal than their contemporary peers,” Tong and Prelogar argue.

    Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, a Democrat, emphasizes the importance of prohibiting assault weapons in her jurisdiction of 5 million people.

    “It’s not a coincidence that 11 of the most populous states in the country have a ban on assault weapons,” Burke claims in an interview. “And the reason for that is because the capabilities of these weapons are not appropriate for densely populated urban areas.”.

    Bullets fired from an AR-15 “have a significantly greater lethal capability,” she adds. “When someone is shot with an AR-15, the damage to the human body is so significant that it’s much more likely to be lethal.”.

    Recent findings suggest that there was some eleventh-hour drama in the Cook County case, with the lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asking to be dismissed from the case. His motion did not explain why.

    In a recent development, in response, Cook County argued that the only other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, lacks standing because he does not seek to own an AR-15 but instead an IMI Galil-Israeli rifle that is modeled on the AK-47. Because of that, Burke states she was obligated to file a suggestion of mootness for the case, which would leave only the Connecticut law at problem.

    Sack of the Second Amendment Foundation declined to say why Viramontes was seeking out of the case, but his group filed a response arguing that the IMI Galil-Israeli rifle is covered by the question presented in the case, and that the second challenger now also seeks to own an AR-15.

    On Nov. 23, the Supreme Court agreed to dismiss Viramontes from the Cook County case, and designated Khaya as the lead petitioner. A day later, the court stated it would consider the mootness question at oral argument.

    Winkler of the UCLA School of Law notes the central issue in the case, while generating a lot of heat, may be of more importance symbolically than in reality. Despite their use in several high-profile mass shootings, AR-15s are relatively rarely used in criminal activity, he says. And with only 11 states prohibiting them, they remain legal in most of the country.

    But if the court upholds these bans, that will energize gun rights activists, he notes.

    But “if it strikes them down, it will motivate gun rights activists to become even more mobilized politically,” possibly prodding them to refocus on other ideas for reducing gun violence more broadly, Winkler says.

    In either event, Winkler says, “whatever the Supreme Court does here will necessarily get far more public attention than other recent decisions by the court on the Second Amendment.”.

    The proposed order bars Shein from making claims about supplier audits or cotton traceability without a reasonable basis.

    Industry observers note that shein has agreed to waive its right to appeal or otherwise challenge the order. If a judge signs it, the court would keep the authority to enforce it.

    A judge found the governor's office failed to prove executive privilege covers the records, rejecting its broad "candid private advice" pitch to keep them secret.

    (CN) â Iowa Governor Kim Reynoldsâ office must turn over four withheld staff communication emails to the stateâs largest newspaper, an Iowa county judge ruled in an order released Tuesday.

    The Des Moines Register has long sought records surrounding Reynoldsâ appearance before a House panel, where she testified on states’ efforts paralleling those of the White Houseâs Department of Government Efficiency.

    The paper prevailed on the bottom line in the order â which was issued Monday â as Polk County District Judge Jason Walke ruled Reynoldsâ office failed to prove executive privilege shields the underlying documents.

    The judge notably held the Iowa Office of the Governor does enjoy some level of executive privilege in specific circumstances under state law, just not in this case.

    In order to obtain such privilege against producing open records, Walke held the office must show âclear and convincing evidenceâ that disclosure would not be in the public interest and would âsubstantially and irreparablyâ limit the executive branchâs ability to function.

    Upon reviewing all four withheld documents covering topics like government efficiency, immigration, gender identity, diversity, equity and inclusion and education funding, Walke found the office did not meet this heavy burden as those matters have been of public interest for years.

    The judge ordered the office to produce the requested documents within 30 days.

    Reynoldsâ office asked the judge in an August summary judgment hearing to declare the emails protected by the same privilege awarded to Iowa General Assembly members â arguing that âcandid adviceâ between the governor and her advisers should be shielded.

    In a snarky rebuttal, Walke noted candid is just another way to say âexpressing opinions, feelings or thoughts.â.

    âThose statements of the executive privilege are, to be blunt, so vague and varied as to be of really no assistance,â Walke said in the ruling, noting that interpretation of executive privilege would apply to an email advising the governor to consider serving âhealthy oatmealâ at state functions instead of âunhealthy pop tarts.â.

    âThat would, after all, be âcandid advice to the governor,’â he added.

    During the relevant February 2025 hearing, U.S. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, asked Reynolds whether she agreed with claims by former Trump adviser Michael Flynn and then-DOGE head Elon Musk that Lutheran Family Services and its affiliates were a âmoney-laundering operation.â.

    After the hearing, the Register filed an open-records request with Reynoldsâ office seeking staff emails mentioning âLutheranâ and âmoney laundering,â as well as any communications with Lutheran Services of Iowa CEO Renee Hardman.

    Reynoldsâ office turned over hundreds of documents, but refused to hand over four specific emails identified by the office as âmedia-prepâ messages â later suing the newspaper in April 2025 to prevent the release of the emails, prompting a swift counterclaim.

    Walke resolved the matter as a whole in his order and cancelled a scheduled December trial, though the possibility of an appeal looms even as Reynolds is set to leave office in under two months time.

    Though Reynoldsâ office lost its bid to withhold the records, Walkeâs order settled that executive privilege exists under state statute, and laid out how courts evaluate it using existing open records law.

    âThis ruling would be the same if the party seeking the docs was not one of the most respected newspapers in the country,â Walke wrote.

    He added that records the governor did not personally read or write are not automatically excluded from executive privilege.

    The Register previously argued executive privilege does not exist in Iowa â noting legislative privilege involves communications between lawmakers and constituents, not between government staffers.

    Walke rejected the paperâs request for attorney fees, damages or other penalties, finding the governorâs office acted in good faith in seeking an injunction over an unsettled legal question.

    Reynolds’ office did not respond to an initial request for comment, and the Register referred to its article published Tuesday in lieu of comment.

    Experts warn public urgency will fade rapidly if health care officials don't practice more consistent, year round engagement with patients and the broader public.

    (CN) â Public opinion is swinging back in favor of childhood vaccines as measles, once eradicated from the U.S., makes a comeback across the continent.

    Sources indicate that truncating a downward slope since 2001, 72% of respondents to a Gallup poll released Tuesday called childhood vaccinations âvery importantâ or âextremely crucial,â compared to 69% in 2024. The share of those who answered âextremely importantâ rose by seven percentage points.

    According to recent reports, gallup released the data, collected in early October, just one week after world health officials revealed that the U.S. has lost its measles-free status. The highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread â largely among the unvaccinated â at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

    Industry observers note that there have been 43 new outbreaks and at least 5,838 confirmed cases of measles across the country in 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As the virus ravages communities, only 17% of respondents said they believed vaccines to be more dangerous than the diseases they prevent â statistically similar to 2024âs results but a far cry from the mere 6% who believed so in 2001.

    The reversal comes after more than a year of outbreaks and efforts by the Trump administration to revoke federal childhood vaccine recommendations, which resulted in multiple lawsuits still working through the courts.

    Jyoti Pathak, dean of Arizona State Universityâs School of Technology for Public Health, remarked public trust naturally ebbs and flows with the current level of exposure.

    âVaccines are often victims of their own success,â Pathak said in an interview. âWhen measles stayed largely out of sight for decades, many parents naturally focused on potential side effects rather than an illness they rarely encountered. As U.S. measles cases reach a 35-year high and local exposure notices hit communities across the country, the real-world risks of hospitalization and severe complications become tangible again.â.

    Pathak warned that while recent outbreaks may wake people up, public urgency fades just as rapidly as it enters the headlines, like it did during the smaller spike in 2019.

    Sustaining confidence after the immediate threat subsides requires moving away from reactive, crisis-only warnings toward consistent, year-round engagement led by trusted âlocal messengers like pediatricians, school nurses and community health workers,â Pathak noted.

    Still, attitudes about childhood vaccinations remain less favorable than in earlier decades. In 2001, 94% of people mentioned vaccinations were very or extremely important. And a large gap still remains between Republicans and Democrats.

    Just 50% of Republicans believe that vaccines are very key, compared to 91% of Democrats. The data also highlights that Republicans are more likely to say theyâve heard only about the negative effects of vaccines and have not heard about the benefits.

    Pathak declined to look at the problem through a purely partisan lens, instead blaming a broader shift against institutional trust fueled in part by fragmented information ecosystems.

    âOver the past decade â and accelerating sharply during the Covid-19 pandemic â public health guidance became entangled in wider debates over mandates, while algorithmic social media feeds sorted Americans into very different information environments,â Pathak mentioned.

    To close the gap in vaccine confidence, Pathak indicates public health experts must âlisten to familiesâ specific questions without judgment, communicate openly about both protective benefits and rare side effects, and use modern data/technology tools to spot emerging confusion early.â.

    âTop-down directives and dense statistical tables rarely persuade worried parents,â he added.

    In November 2025, Kennedy Jr. directed the CDC to revise its website to suggest a connection between vaccines and autism, a departure from previous guidance. President Donald Trump also linked the childhood vaccine schedule and autism while signing an executive order that revised vaccine recommendations in August 2026.

    While those who do not believe vaccines cause autism rose from 36% to 46% since 2024, 16% of respondents say they believe vaccines do cause autism â the highest percentage since 2015.

    It has been revealed that âSocial media stories still travel much faster than epidemiological studies â especially when parents navigating an autism diagnosis are searching online for answers,â Pathak mentioned. âData alone is not enough unless clinicians and public health communicators share it with empathy, clarity and respect.â.

    Just in the U.S., the CDC estimates routine childhood vaccinations have prevented approximately 508 million cases of illness, 32 million hospitalizations and over 1.1 million deaths, generating $2.7 trillion in societal savings.

    Associate Clinical Professor Nicole Ferschke at Northern Arizona University mentioned vaccination is one of the best ways to prevent the further spread of measles.

    âIt protects the person who is vaccinated as well as contributes to herd immunity, which protects individuals who cannot be vaccinated for specific medical reasons,â she told Courthouse News.

    Ferschke echoed Pathakâs concerns that the short-term uptick will not be sustained without increased efforts to improve trust in healthcare nationwide, which includes increasing access to vaccines and transparent, evidence-based communication.

    Appeals court rules Arizona media outlets can publish statements made by daughters of accused murderer

    • According to recent reports, “We are troubled that no one told the daughters the consequences of reading their statements in open court,” wrote Judge Jennifer Perkins in the unanimous opinion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A judge had issued a "gag order," barring the media from reporting on what was mentioned in open court by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti.

    (CN) â The Arizona Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that news organizations can publish statements made, in open court, by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti, who is accused of shooting his estranged wife to death.

    According to recent reports, “We are troubled that no one told the daughters the consequences of reading their statements in open court,” wrote Judge Jennifer Perkins in the unanimous opinion. “But once the daughters spoke in open court, the First Amendment protected the pressâs right to publish what they said, even if the failure to warn the daughters was inconsistent with the Victimsâ Bill of Rights.”.

    Abatti, a 63-year-old prominent farmer, is charged with first-degree murder in the death of his wife, 59-year-old Kerri Ann Abatti. The Imperial Valley couple had been embroiled in a bitter, three-year-long divorce, at the heart of which lay a $200 million trust. Arrested four weeks after the shooting, Abatti pleaded not guilty and is being held in custody, apparently unable to post the $5.5 million in bail.

    At Abatti’s arraignment in December last year, his two daughters, who attended the hearing remotely, were allowed to read victim impact statements. A reporter from KPNX-TV Channel 12 was also listening to the proceedings remotely, with the court’s approval. The daughters’ statements were admitted into the record under seal, but they were also allowed to read them aloud during the hearing, which was open to the public. After the first statement was read, both the prosecutor and the defense attorney asked the court to issue a “gag order,” barring members of the media from reporting what the daughters mentioned.

    KPNX objected to the gag order, arguing it was unconstitutional prior restraint. But both Abatti and his daughters urged the judge to stand by the order, Abatti arguing that publishing the statements would taint the small-town jury pool, and the daughters arguing they didn’t know the hearing was a public forum. The judge kept the gag order in place, and KPNX, joined by a handful of other local media outlets, filed a petition to overrule the order.

    According to recent reports, the three-judge panel found the gag order was unconstitutional under both the Arizona and U.S. Constitutions.

    “A court may not bar the press from publishing what happens in open court unless the ‘gravity of the evil’ resulting from publication, ‘discounted by its improbability, justifies such invasion of free speech as is necessary to avoid the danger,’” Perkins wrote, citing a 1976 Supreme Court ruling.

    As to the argument that the daughters’ statements would taint the jury pool, Perkins wrote, “Even if the small, rural community here increases the risk of jury prejudice, that risk remains too speculative … Abatti has not shown, for example, that ordinary tools â a larger jury pool, questioning prospective jurors about media exposure, and instructing jurors to consider only the trial evidence â would fail to protect him from prejudice caused by reporting on his daughtersâ statements.”.

    The panel found that while the daughters might be harmed by the publicizing of their comments, “the gravity of the potential emotional harm to the adult daughters does not justify the prior restraint.”.

    Judges Jon Saline and Samuel Clark rounded out the panel.

    #101425. What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?
